entities.name: Comita of Gallura
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Comita of Gallura, who reigned as Judge (Latin: Iudex) from approximately 1133 until his death in 1146, was a pivotal figure in the complex political landscape of medieval Sardinia. As a member of the Lacon-Gunale dynasty, he governed one of the island's four autonomous Judicates, maintaining its sovereignty amidst the competing ambitions of the powerful maritime republics of Pisa and Genoa. His reign is significant for solidifying Gallura's internal stability and strategically aligning the Judicate with Pisa, a relationship that profoundly influenced Sardinian politics and commerce throughout the 12th century. His actions contributed to the unique development of Sardinian self-governance, distinct from mainland Italian feudal systems.

Ascending to power following the death of his predecessor, Costantino II, Comita's rule was characterized by careful diplomatic maneuvering and internal consolidation. One of his defining acts was the formal renewal of Gallura's allegiance to the Archdiocese of Pisa in 1133, a strategic move that secured ecclesiastical and military support against potential Genoese incursions and internal rivals. This alliance was cemented by his participation in the Pisan-led Synod of Pisa in 1135, where he, alongside other Sardinian Judges, acknowledged Pisan ecclesiastical supremacy over the island. He also focused on maintaining the Carta de Logu (charter of laws), an important legal framework, ensuring the continued judicial and administrative autonomy of his Judicate. His reign saw the continued construction and patronage of churches and monasteries, reinforcing the Christian identity of Gallura.
